statements.title: Density of Points for Smooth Schemes Under Completion
statements.statement_plain: For a discretely valued Henselian field k and its ring of integers o, rational points of every smooth k-scheme are dense after mapping to the completion, and integral points of every smooth o-scheme are dense in the corresponding completed integral model.
statements.statement_latex: Let k be a discretely valued Henselian field with ring of integers \mathfrak{o}, and let \widehat{k},\widehat{\mathfrak{o}} denote the respective completions. (1) If X is a smooth k-scheme, the image of X(k) in X(\widehat{k}) is dense. (2) If \mathcal{X} is a smooth \mathfrak{o}-scheme, the image of \mathcal{X}(\mathfrak{o}) in \mathcal{X}(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}}) is dense.
assumptions_latex: k is a discretely valued Henselian field.
\mathfrak{o} is the ring of integers of k.
\widehat{k} and \widehat{\mathfrak{o}} are the completions of k and \mathfrak{o}, respectively.
statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(1) For every smooth }k\text{-scheme }X,\;\operatorname{im}\bigl(X(k)\to X(\widehat{k})\bigr)\text{ is dense.}\quad\text{(2) For every smooth }\mathfrak{o}\text{-scheme }\mathcal{X},\;\operatorname{im}\bigl(\mathcal{X}(\mathfrak{o})\to\mathcal{X}(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})\bigr)\text{ is dense}.
statements.scope_note: Density of rational and integral points under completion for smooth schemes over a discretely valued Henselian field and its ring of integers.

statements.title: Equivalence of Henselianity for a Valued Field and Its Valuation Ring
statements.statement_plain: A field k with real-valued valuation omega is Henselian exactly when its valuation ring o = {x in k : omega(x) >= 0} satisfies Hensel's lemma.
statements.statement_latex: For a field \(k\) equipped with a valuation \(\omega:k^{\times}\to\mathbf{R}\), the following are equivalent: (1) \(k\) is Henselian; (2) the valuation ring \(\mathfrak{o}=\{x\in k\mid \omega(x)\ge 0\}\) is Henselian in the sense that Hensel's lemma holds.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is a field equipped with a valuation \(\omega:k^{\times}\to\mathbf{R}\).
statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\) is Henselian if and only if its valuation ring \(\mathfrak{o}=\{x\in k\mid \omega(x)\ge 0\}\) is Henselian, meaning that Hensel's lemma holds for \(\mathfrak{o}\).
statements.scope_note: Equivalence between Henselianity of a valued field and the Hensel property of its valuation ring.

statements.title: Finite separable extensions and Galois groups under Henselian completion
statements.statement_plain: For a Henselian valued field k and its completion, each finite separable extension satisfies the natural tensor-product isomorphism with the completion. Completion gives an equivalence between finite separable extensions of k and of the completion, and, after compatible separable closures are embedded, identifies the absolute Galois groups.
statements.statement_latex: Let k be a Henselian valued field with completion \widehat{k}. For every finite separable extension \ell/k, the natural map \ell\otimes_k\widehat{k}\to\widehat{\ell} is an isomorphism. After fixing an embedding k_s\hookrightarrow(\widehat{k})_s over k\to\widehat{k}, the correspondence \ell\mapsto\widehat{\ell} induces an equivalence between the categories of finite separable extensions of k and of \widehat{k}, and yields a canonical identification \operatorname{Gal}(k_s/k)\cong\operatorname{Gal}((\widehat{k})_s/\widehat{k}).
assumptions_latex: k is a Henselian valued field with completion \widehat{k}
\ell/k is a finite separable extension
An embedding k_s\hookrightarrow(\widehat{k})_s over k\to\widehat{k} is fixed
statements.conclusion_latex: \ell\otimes_k\widehat{k}\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat{\ell};\quad \ell\mapsto\widehat{\ell}\text{ induces an equivalence between the categories of finite separable extensions of }k\text{ and }\widehat{k};\quad \operatorname{Gal}(k_s/k)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Gal}((\widehat{k})_s/\widehat{k})
statements.scope_note: In the Henselian valued-field setting of Section 2.1, completion preserves finite separable extensions and identifies the corresponding absolute Galois groups after compatible separable closures are embedded.

statements.title: Henselian valuation extension and ramification-index definition
statements.statement_plain: Assume k has a non-archimedean discrete valuation whose valuation ring is Henselian and whose residue field is perfect. The valuation extends uniquely to every algebraic extension and is denoted by the same symbol. For each finite extension ell of k, the ramification index is the index of the value group of k in the value group of ell.

Then \(\omega\) extends uniquely to any algebraic extension of \(k\), and all such extensions are also denoted by \(\omega\). For a finite extension \(\ell/k\), its ramification index is \[e(\ell/k)=\left[\omega(\ell^{\times}):\omega(k^{\times})\right].\]

statements.title: Definitions of total and tame ramification
statements.statement_plain: Let k be discretely non-archimedean valued with Henselian valuation ring and perfect residue field. The valuation extends uniquely to algebraic extensions. For a finite extension ell over k, e(ell/k) is the index of value groups [omega(ell^times):omega(k^times)]. It is totally ramified when this index equals [ell:k], and tamely ramified when the residue characteristic does not divide the index. In residue characteristic zero, every finite algebraic extension is tame.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be a field with non-archimedean discrete valuation \(\omega\), Henselian valuation ring \(\mathfrak d\), and perfect residue field \(\mathfrak f\). The valuation extends uniquely to every algebraic extension of \(k\). For finite \(\ell/k\), set \(e(\ell/k)=[\omega(\ell^{\times}):\omega(k^{\times})]\). We call \(\ell/k\) totally ramified when \(e(\ell/k)=[\ell:k]\), and tamely ramified when \(\operatorname{char}(\mathfrak f)\) does not divide \(e(\ell/k)\); when \(\operatorname{char}(\mathfrak f)=0\), every finite algebraic extension of \(k\) is tamely ramified.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) has a non-archimedean discrete valuation \(\omega\) whose valuation ring \(\mathfrak d\) is Henselian and whose residue field \(\mathfrak f\) is perfect.
statements.conclusion_latex: The valuation \(\omega\) extends uniquely to every algebraic extension of \(k\). For a finite extension \(\ell/k\), total ramification is defined by \(e(\ell/k)=[\ell:k]\), and tame ramification is defined by \(\operatorname{char}(\mathfrak f)\nmid e(\ell/k)\). If \(\operatorname{char}(\mathfrak f)=0\), every finite algebraic extension of \(k\) is tamely ramified.
statements.scope_note: Definitions for finite algebraic extensions of a Henselian discretely valued field with perfect residue field, in the tamely ramified descent setting.

statements.title: Inertia and Wild Inertia Subgroups
statements.statement_plain: Let ell over k be a finite or infinite Galois extension, and assume every Galois automorphism preserves the valuation omega. The automorphisms stabilize the valuation ring and maximal ideal and act on the residue field f_ell. Inertia is the subgroup acting trivially on f_ell; wild inertia is the subgroup of automorphisms sigma for which omega(x minus sigma(x)) is greater than omega(x) for every nonzero x in ell.
statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\ell/k\) be a finite or infinite Galois extension. Let \(\mathfrak f_\ell\) and \(\mathfrak f\) be the residue fields of \(\ell\) and \(k\), respectively. Assume every \(\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k)\) preserves \(\omega\). Then each \(\sigma\) stabilizes \(\mathfrak o_\ell\) and its maximal ideal and induces an action \(\left.\sigma\right|_{\mathfrak f_\ell}\) on \(\mathfrak f_\ell\). The inertia and wild inertia subgroups are defined by
\[
I(\ell/k)=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k):\left.\sigma\right|_{\mathfrak f_\ell}=1\},
\qquad
W(\ell/k)=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k):\omega(x-\sigma(x))>\omega(x)\text{ for all }x\in\ell^\times\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \ell/k\text{ is a finite or infinite Galois extension}
\text{Every }\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k)\text{ preserves the valuation }\omega
statements.conclusion_latex: I(\ell/k)=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k):\left.\sigma\right|_{\mathfrak f_\ell}=1\},\qquad W(\ell/k)=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k):\omega(x-\sigma(x))>\omega(x)\ \text{for all }x\in\ell^\times\}.
statements.scope_note: Here \(\mathfrak f_\ell\) and \(\mathfrak f\) are the residue fields of \(\ell\) and \(k\), respectively. Valuation preservation implies that each automorphism stabilizes \(\mathfrak o_\ell\) and its maximal ideal and therefore induces the indicated residue-field action.

statements.title: Strict Henselization inside an admissible Galois extension
statements.statement_plain: Let K be Henselian and L/K an admissible Galois extension, with L_t its maximal etale subextension. A strict Henselization K' of K containing L_t, equivalently a maximal etale extension of L_t unique up to isomorphism, satisfies K' intersect L = L_t. Its residue field is a separable closure of the residue field of L_t and is linearly disjoint from the residue field of L over the residue field of L intersect K'; the residue extension of L over L_t is purely inseparable.

Then K'\cap L=L_t, and the residue field \overline{K'} is a separable closure of \overline{L_t} linearly disjoint from \overline{L} over \overline{L\cap K'}, while \overline{L}/\overline{L_t} is purely inseparable.

statements.title: Group Scheme Extension Defined by a 2-Cocycle
statements.statement_plain: For a 2-cocycle f from G_M times G_M to G_N with trivial action, the twisted product G_M times_f G_N is a group scheme with the displayed cocycle multiplication. G_N embeds as a closed normal subgroup, the quotient is G_M by projection, and the extension is commutative if and only if f is symmetric bilinear.

assumptions_latex: f:G_M\times G_M\to G_N\text{ is a 2-cocycle for the trivial action of }G_M\text{ on }G_N.
statements.conclusion_latex: G_M\times_f G_N\text{ has multiplication }(x_1,y_1)(x_2,y_2)=(x_1+x_2,\,y_1+y_2+f(x_1,x_2));\ G_N\to G_M\times_f G_N,\ y\mapsto(0,y),\text{ is a closed immersion with normal image; }(G_M\times_f G_N)/G_N\cong G_M\text{ via }(x,y)\mapsto x;\ G_M\times_f G_N\text{ is commutative iff }f\text{ is symmetric bilinear}.

statements.title: Conjugacy of Parabolic Cocharacters into a Torus
statements.statement_plain: Let H be a smooth connected affine algebraic F-group and Q a parabolic F-subgroup. If an F-torus S in Q maps to a subgroup containing the maximal central torus of the reductive quotient Q/Ru(Q), then every cocharacter lambda of H with Q equal to P_H(lambda)Ru(H) can be conjugated by an F-point of Ru(Q) to a cocharacter whose image lies in S.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a smooth connected affine algebraic \(F\)-group, \(\mathcal Q\) a parabolic \(F\)-subgroup, and \(\mathcal S\subset\mathcal Q\) an \(F\)-torus whose image in \(\mathcal Q/\mathcal R_u(\mathcal Q)\) contains the maximal central torus of this quotient. Every one-parameter subgroup \(\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to\mathcal H\) satisfying \(\mathcal Q=P_{\mathcal H}(\lambda)\mathcal R_u(\mathcal H)\) is conjugate by an element of \(\mathcal R_u(\mathcal Q)(F)\) to a one-parameter subgroup with image in \(\mathcal S\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a smooth connected affine algebraic \(F\)-group.
\(\mathcal Q\subset\mathcal H\) is a parabolic \(F\)-subgroup.
\(\mathcal S\) is an \(F\)-torus of \(\mathcal Q\) whose image in \(\mathcal Q/\mathcal R_u(\mathcal Q)\) contains the maximal central torus of that reductive quotient.
\(\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to\mathcal H\) is a one-parameter subgroup satisfying \(\mathcal Q=P_{\mathcal H}(\lambda)\mathcal R_u(\mathcal H)\).
statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(u\in\mathcal R_u(\mathcal Q)(F)\) such that \(t\mapsto u\lambda(t)u^{-1}\) has image contained in \(\mathcal S\).
statements.scope_note: Conjugacy, by an F-point of the unipotent radical of a parabolic subgroup, of a cocharacter defining that parabolic up to the unipotent radical of the ambient group into a chosen torus whose reductive-quotient image contains the maximal central torus.

statements.title: Quasi-reductive groups and maximal quasi-reductive quotients
statements.statement_plain: For a connected smooth affine group H over a field k, define its k-unipotent radical and k-split unipotent radical as the maximal smooth connected normal unipotent and k-split unipotent k-subgroups, respectively. The split radical is the maximal connected k-split subgroup of the ordinary radical. H is quasi-reductive exactly when its split radical is trivial. Quotienting by the split radical gives the maximal quasi-reductive quotient; its unipotent radical is the corresponding quotient and is k-wound, so toral actions on it are trivial. In the quasi-reductive case every k-torus of H commutes with the unipotent radical. The induced map on k-points is surjective. Over a perfect field, the quasi-reductive quotient is the maximal reductive quotient.
statements.statement_latex: For a connected smooth affine k-group H, define \(\mathcal R_{u,k}(H)\) as the maximal smooth connected normal unipotent k-subgroup and \(\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)\) as the maximal smooth connected normal k-split unipotent k-subgroup; \(\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)\) is the maximal connected k-split subgroup of \(\mathcal R_{u,k}(H)\). H is quasi-reductive iff \(\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)=1\). The quotient \(H^{\mathrm{qred}}:=H/\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)\) is the maximal quasi-reductive quotient, and \(\mathcal R_{u,k}(H^{\mathrm{qred}})=\mathcal R_{u,k}(H)/\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)\) is k-wound (there is no nontrivial homomorphism \(\mathbf G_a\to\mathcal R_{u,k}(H^{\mathrm{qred}})\)); every toral action on this wound group is trivial. If H is quasi-reductive, then \(\mathcal R_{u,k}(H)\) is k-wound and every k-torus of H commutes with it. Since \(\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)\) is k-split, \(H^1(k,\mathcal R_{us,k}(H))=1\), so \(H(k)\to H^{\mathrm{qred}}(k)\) is surjective. If k is perfect, then \(\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)=\mathcal R_u(H)\), and \(H^{\mathrm{qred}}\) is reductive, hence the maximal reductive quotient of H.
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is a field}
H\text{ is a connected smooth affine }k\text{-group}
statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R_{us,k}(H)\subseteq\mathcal R_{u,k}(H),\quad H\text{ quasi-reductive}\Longleftrightarrow\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)=1,\quad H^{\mathrm{qred}}:=H/\mathcal R_{us,k}(H),\quad \mathcal R_{u,k}(H^{\mathrm{qred}})=\mathcal R_{u,k}(H)/\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)\text{ is }k\text{-wound},\quad \text{all toral actions on it are trivial};\quad H\text{ quasi-reductive}\Rightarrow\text{every }k\text{-torus of }H\text{ commutes with }\mathcal R_{u,k}(H);\quad H^1(k,\mathcal R_{us,k}(H))=1\Rightarrow H(k)\twoheadrightarrow H^{\mathrm{qred}}(k);\quad k\text{ perfect}\Rightarrow\mathcal R_{us,k}(H)=\mathcal R_u(H)\text{ and }H^{\mathrm{qred}}\text{ is the maximal reductive quotient}.
statements.scope_note: Defines the ordinary and k-split unipotent radicals and quasi-reductivity, then states the maximal quasi-reductive quotient and the explicitly given woundness, torus-centralization, k-point surjectivity, and perfect-field consequences.

statements.statement_plain: For an R-module M, the functor sending each R-algebra A to the additive group of M tensor_R A is represented by the affine scheme Spec of the symmetric algebra on M's dual. Such an affine algebraic group is called a vector group.

statements.title: Weights of Generated and Commutator Subgroups
statements.statement_plain: Let H1 and H2 be smooth connected k-subgroups stable under the S-action, let H be the subgroup they generate, and let [H1,H2] be their commutator subgroup. The weights of H form the subsemigroup of X*(S) generated by the weights of H1 and H2, while every weight of [H1,H2] lies in the sumset of the weights of H1 and H2.

statements.title: Canonical tori in a quasi-split reductive group
statements.statement_plain: For a quasi-split reductive group G over k, let S' be a maximal k-split torus in the derived subgroup. Let S be the unique maximal k-split torus of G containing S', and let T be the unique maximal torus of G containing S' (equivalently, S). Then S equals S' exactly when the center of G is anisotropic, and S equals T exactly when G is split. Each of S', S, and T determines the other two. Define T_der as T intersected with G_der.
statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }G/k\text{ be quasi-split reductive. Let }S'\text{ be a maximal }k\text{-split torus in }G_{\mathrm{der}},\ S\text{ the unique maximal }k\text{-split torus of }G\text{ containing }S',\text{ and }T\text{ the unique maximal torus of }G\text{ containing }S'\text{ (equivalently, }S\text{). Then }S=S'\iff Z(G)\text{ is anisotropic, and }S=T\iff G\text{ is split. Each of }S',S,T\text{ determines the other two; define }T_{\mathrm{der}}=T\cap G_{\mathrm{der}}.
assumptions_latex: G/k is a quasi-split reductive group.
S' is a maximal k-split torus in G_{\mathrm{der}}.
S is the unique maximal k-split torus of G containing S'.
T is the unique maximal torus of G containing S' (equivalently, containing S).
statements.conclusion_latex: S=S'\Longleftrightarrow Z(G)\text{ is anisotropic},\qquad S=T\Longleftrightarrow G\text{ is split};\qquad S',S,T\text{ each determine the other two};\qquad T_{\mathrm{der}}:=T\cap G_{\mathrm{der}}.
statements.scope_note: Canonical torus notation and relationships for a quasi-split reductive group over k.

statements.title: Minisotropic (Elliptic) Tori
statements.statement_plain: For a reductive group H over a field F, an F-torus T is minisotropic, or elliptic, when the maximal torus in T intersected with the derived group H_der is F-anisotropic. assumptions_latex: F is a field.
H is a reductive F-group.
T is an F-torus of H; for the equivalence below, T is a maximal F-torus of H.
statements.conclusion_latex: An F-torus T of H is minisotropic (or elliptic) if the maximal torus contained in T\cap H_{\mathrm{der}} is F-anisotropic. If T is a maximal F-torus of H, then T is minisotropic if and only if H contains no proper parabolic F-subgroup containing T.

statements.title: Restriction-of-scalars torus and maximal split subtorus
statements.statement_plain: For a finite extension L/K of degree d and a Galois extension K'/K containing L, the restriction-of-scalars torus T = Pi_{L/K} Mult becomes Mult^d over K'. Its character group is Z^d with a Galois-permuted basis indexed by Gal(K'/K)/Gal(K'/L). The smallest Galois splitting field is the normal closure of L/K, and T is split over K exactly when L=K. The K-rational characters are the integer multiples of the norm character N_{L/K}; the maximal K-split subtorus is one-dimensional and equals the canonical image of Mult.
statements.statement_latex: Let L/K be finite of degree d and let K'/K be Galois with L\subseteq K'. For \mathbf T=\Pi_{L/K}\mathrm{Mult}, the base change \mathbf T_{K'} is isomorphic to \mathrm{Mult}_{K'}^{d}. The character group X(\mathbf T)\simeq\mathbf Z^d has a basis indexed by I=\operatorname{Gal}(K'/K)/\operatorname{Gal}(K'/L), permuted by the Galois action. The smallest Galois splitting field is the normal closure of L/K, and \mathbf T is K-split exactly when L=K. Moreover X(\mathbf T)^{\operatorname{Gal}(K'/K)}=\mathbf Z\,N_{L/K}, and the maximal K-split subtorus is one-dimensional, equal to the canonical diagonal image of \mathrm{Mult}.
assumptions_latex: L/K is a finite extension of degree d.
K'/K is a Galois extension containing L.
statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf T=\Pi_{L/K}\mathrm{Mult} is a K-torus split over K' with \mathbf T_{K'}\simeq\mathrm{Mult}_{K'}^{d}; its character group is \mathbf Z^{d} with a Galois-stable basis (\chi_i)_{i\in I}, where I=\operatorname{Gal}(K'/K)/\operatorname{Gal}(K'/L). The smallest Galois extension of K splitting \mathbf T is the Galois (normal) closure generated by L, and \mathbf T is split over K if and only if L=K. The K-rational characters are \mathbf Z\left(\sum_{i\in I}\chi_i\right)=\mathbf Z\,N_{L/K}. The maximal K-split subtorus has dimension 1 and is the canonical image of \mathrm{Mult} in \Pi_{L/K}\mathrm{Mult}.
statements.scope_note: Restriction-of-scalars torus, its Galois character module and norm character, splitting field, and maximal K-split subtorus.

statements.title: Weight-Space Decomposition of a Stable Projective A-Submodule
statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional K-representation of a K-defined split torus, a projective A-submodule that spans the representation and is stable under the canonical A-group-scheme extension decomposes as the direct sum of its intersections with the ordered weight spaces. Each weight space is generated over K by its corresponding submodule summand.
statements.statement_latex: Let V be finite-dimensional over K, let S be a K-defined split torus in \mathrm{GL}(V), and let M be a projective A-submodule with K\otimes_A M\cong V, stable under the canonical A-group scheme extending S. Ordering the S-weights \alpha_i increasingly and writing V_i for the corresponding weight spaces, one has M=\bigoplus_i(M\cap V_i) and V_i=K(M\cap V_i).
assumptions_latex: V is a finite-dimensional K-vector space and S is a K-defined split torus in \mathrm{GL}(V).
M is a projective A-submodule of V such that the canonical map K\otimes_A M\to V is an isomorphism.
The canonical A-group scheme extending S acts on M.
A total order compatible with addition is chosen on X^*(S); \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n are the ordered S-weights in V, with V_i the \alpha_i-weight space.
statements.conclusion_latex: M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}M_i\quad\text{where }M_i=M\cap V_i,\qquad V_i=K M_i\quad(1\le i\le n).
statements.scope_note: Integral weight-space decomposition under a split torus action on a projective A-submodule spanning the K-representation.

statements.title: Split Unipotent Radical and Root-Product Decomposition
statements.statement_plain: The split unipotent radical R_ud(G) is the largest unipotent subgroup contained in the radical of G that is defined and split over K. Over a perfect K it is the unipotent radical of the source's group G. It is distinguished and stable under separable extensions. The positive-root intersections, the split unipotent radical of the center, and the negative-root intersections multiply to R_ud(G) through an isomorphism of K-varieties, each root intersection being K-split unipotent. For every closed root subset Psi satisfying (-Psi) intersected with Phi is contained in Psi, R_ud(G_Psi) equals R_ud(G) intersected with G_Psi.
statements.statement_latex: The split unipotent radical \(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\) is the largest unipotent subgroup defined and split over \(K\) contained in the radical of \(G\). If \(K\) is perfect, it equals the unipotent radical of \(\mathbf G\); it is distinguished and stable under separable extensions of \(K\), its positive-root, central, and negative-root factors multiply K-variety-isomorphically onto \(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\), and for every closed \(\Psi\subset\Phi\) with \((-\Psi)\cap\Phi\subseteq\Psi\), \(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G_{\Psi})=R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\cap G_{\Psi}\).
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is an algebraic group over a field \(K\), with root system \(\Phi\), positive and negative root sets \(\Phi^{+},\Phi^{-}\), root subgroups \(U_a\), center \(Z\), and associated subgroups \(G_{\Psi}\).
\(\Psi\subset\Phi\) is closed and satisfies \((-\Psi)\cap\Phi\subseteq\Psi\).
statements.conclusion_latex: The split unipotent radical \(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\) is the largest unipotent subgroup of the radical of \(G\) that is defined and split over \(K\). If \(K\) is perfect, it is the unipotent radical of \(\mathbf G\). It is a distinguished subgroup stable under separable extensions of \(K\). The ordered product map \(\prod_{a\in\Phi^{+}}(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\cap U_a)\times R_{\mathrm{ud}}(Z)\times\prod_{a\in\Phi^{-}}(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\cap U_a)\to R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\) is an isomorphism of \(K\)-varieties, each intersection \(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\cap U_a\) is unipotent and split over \(K\), and \(R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G_{\Psi})=R_{\mathrm{ud}}(G)\cap G_{\Psi}\).
statements.scope_note: Definition of the split unipotent radical together with the structural properties explicitly stated in the source; proof-status remarks and citations are omitted.

statements.title: Roots and Root Rays Relative to S
statements.statement_plain: The roots of G relative to S are the nonzero S-weights in the adjoint representation on Lie G. They form a finite subset of X*(S), viewed in E = R tensor X*(S). A root ray is an open half-line in E from the origin containing at least one root, and the set of root rays is denoted Phi(S,G), or Phi.
statements.statement_latex: The roots of \(\mathrm{G}\) with respect to \(\mathrm{S}\) are the nonzero \(\mathrm{S}\)-weights in the adjoint representation of \(\mathrm{G}\) on \(\operatorname{Lie}\mathrm{G}\). They form a finite subset of the character group \(X^{*}(\mathrm{S})\), identified with its canonical image in \(\mathrm{E}=\mathbf{R}\otimes X^{*}(\mathrm{S})\). A root ray is an open half-line in \(\mathrm{E}\) with origin \(o\) containing at least one root; the set of root rays is denoted \(\Phi(\mathrm{S},\mathrm{G})\) or \(\Phi\).
statements.conclusion_latex: The roots of \(\mathrm{G}\) relative to \(\mathrm{S}\) form a finite subset of \(X^{*}(\mathrm{S})\), and a root ray is an open half-line in \(\mathrm{E}\) with origin \(o\) containing at least one root; the set of root rays is denoted \(\Phi(\mathrm{S},\mathrm{G})\) or \(\Phi\).
statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to S via the adjoint representation of G on Lie G, with X*(S) identified with its canonical image in E.

statements.title: Connected Root Supports and Dynkin Subdiagrams
statements.statement_plain: In a reduced irreducible root system, every root has a connected support in the Dynkin diagram; conversely, summing the simple roots in any connected Dynkin subdiagram gives another root.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be a reduced irreducible root system with simple-root basis \(\Delta\) and Dynkin diagram \(\mathcal{D}\). For any \(\alpha\in\Phi\), the simple roots occurring in its expansion form a connected subdiagram of \(\mathcal{D}\). Conversely, the sum of the simple roots in any connected subdiagram of \(\mathcal{D}\) is a root of \(\Phi\).
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is a reduced irreducible root system.
\(\Delta\) is a basis of simple roots and \(\mathcal{D}\) is its Dynkin diagram.
For \(\alpha\in\Phi\), \(\Delta'\subset\Delta\) is the set of simple roots occurring with nonzero coefficient in the simple-root expansion of \(\alpha\).
statements.conclusion_latex: (1) For every \(\alpha\in\Phi\), the Dynkin subdiagram induced by its simple-root support \(\Delta'\) is connected. (2) Conversely, if \(\Delta'\subset\Delta\) induces a connected Dynkin subdiagram, then \(\sum_{\beta\in\Delta'}\beta\in\Phi\).
statements.scope_note: Combinatorial criterion for supports of roots and connected subdiagrams in a reduced irreducible root system.

statements.title: Maximal Tori and Root Data Under Canonical Isogenies
statements.statement_plain: For a maximal torus T in a connected reductive group G, its intersection with the derived subgroup, inverse image in the simply connected cover, and image in the adjoint quotient are maximal tori. Their absolute root systems are naturally bijective, and the corresponding root groups are isomorphic.
statements.statement_latex: For a maximal torus \(T\) of a connected reductive group \(G\), the torus \(T_{\mathrm{der}}=T\cap G_{\mathrm{der}}\), its inverse image \(T_{\mathrm{sc}}\) in \(G_{\mathrm{sc}}\), and the image \(T_{\mathrm{ad}}\) in \(G_{\mathrm{ad}}\) are maximal tori; the natural maps between their absolute root systems and \(\Phi(T,G)\) are bijections, and corresponding absolute root groups are isomorphic.
assumptions_latex: G is a connected reductive algebraic group with canonical maps \(\pi_{\mathrm{sc}}:G_{\mathrm{sc}}\to G_{\mathrm{der}}\), \(G_{\mathrm{der}}\hookrightarrow G\), and \(G\to G_{\mathrm{ad}}\).
T\subset G is a maximal torus.
statements.conclusion_latex: Define \(T_{\mathrm{der}}:=T\cap G_{\mathrm{der}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{sc}}:=\pi_{\mathrm{sc}}^{-1}(T_{\mathrm{der}})\), and let \(T_{\mathrm{ad}}\) be the image of \(T\) in \(G_{\mathrm{ad}}\). Then these are maximal tori of \(G_{\mathrm{der}},G_{\mathrm{sc}},G_{\mathrm{ad}}\), respectively; the natural maps \(\Phi(T_{\mathrm{sc}},G_{\mathrm{sc}})\to\Phi(T_{\mathrm{der}},G_{\mathrm{der}})\to\Phi(T,G)\to\Phi(T_{\mathrm{ad}},G_{\mathrm{ad}})\) are bijections; and for every \(\widetilde a\in\Phi(T,G)\), the induced maps on the corresponding absolute root groups are isomorphisms.

statements.title: Relative root datum of a quasi-split group
statements.statement_plain: In the setting of Assumption 2.15.15 for a quasi-split group G and an inclusion S into T, the character and cocharacter groups of S are respectively the torsion-free Theta-coinvariants and Theta-invariants of those of T. The relative roots are the restrictions of the absolute roots. No absolute root restricts to zero, and all absolute roots restricting to a given relative root form one Theta-orbit.
statements.statement_latex: Under Assumption 2.15.15, let G be quasi-split and let S\hookrightarrow T be as in that setting. Then S determines the relative root datum \(\bigl(X^*(S),\Phi(S),X_*(S),\Phi(S)^\vee\bigr)\), where \(X^*(S)=X^*(T)_{\Theta,\mathrm{free}}\), \(X_*(S)=X_*(T)^\Theta\), and \(\Phi(S)\) is the image of \(\Phi(T)\) under the restriction map \(X^*(T)\to X^*(S)\). No element of \(\Phi(T)\) lies in the kernel of this map, and the preimage of every element of \(\Phi(S)\) is a single \(\Theta\)-orbit in \(\Phi(T)\).
assumptions_latex: \text{The setting and hypotheses of Assumption 2.15.15 hold for }G,S,T,\Theta.
G\text{ is quasi-split}.
S\hookrightarrow T.
statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(X^*(S),\Phi(S),X_*(S),\Phi(S)^\vee\bigr)\text{ is the relative root datum, with }X^*(S)=X^*(T)_{\Theta,\mathrm{free}},\ X_*(S)=X_*(T)^\Theta,\ \Phi(S)=\operatorname{im}\bigl(\Phi(T)\to X^*(S)\bigr),\ \ker\bigl(X^*(T)\to X^*(S)\bigr)\cap\Phi(T)=\varnothing,\text{ and the preimage of each element of }\Phi(S)\text{ is a single }\Theta\text{-orbit in }\Phi(T).
statements.scope_note: In the setting of Assumption 2.15.15, with quasi-split G and S included in T; the restriction map is induced by S\hookrightarrow T.

statements.title: Relative root system and Weyl group
statements.statement_plain: For any field F, if G is a connected reductive F-group and S is a maximal F-split torus, the S-weights on Lie(G) form the relative root system Phi(S), and N_G(S)(F)/Z_G(S)(F) is its Weyl group.

The finite group W=N_G(S)(F)/Z_G(S)(F) acts on X^*(S) and is identified with the Weyl group of this root system; \Phi(S) is the relative root system of G.

statements.title: Relative roots and root groups under derived, simply connected, and adjoint maps
statements.statement_plain: Let S be a maximal split torus of a reductive group G, with the associated maximal split tori in the derived group, its simply connected cover, and the adjoint quotient. The canonical maps identify the four relative root systems bijectively. For each relative root, they also induce isomorphisms among the corresponding relative root groups.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subset G\) be a maximal split torus. Let \(S_{\mathrm{der}}\) be the maximal split torus of \(G_{\mathrm{der}}\) contained in \(S\), let \(S_{\mathrm{sc}}\) be a maximal split torus of \(G_{\mathrm{sc}}\) whose image in \(G_{\mathrm{der}}\) lies in \(S_{\mathrm{der}}\), and let \(S_{\mathrm{ad}}\) be the image of \(S\) in \(G_{\mathrm{ad}}\). The natural maps \[\Phi(S_{\mathrm{sc}},G_{\mathrm{sc}})\longrightarrow\Phi(S_{\mathrm{der}},G_{\mathrm{der}})\longrightarrow\Phi(S,G)\longrightarrow\Phi(S_{\mathrm{ad}},G_{\mathrm{ad}})\] are bijective. After identifying these root systems with \(\Phi(S,G)\), the canonical maps \(G_{\mathrm{sc}}\to G_{\mathrm{der}}\to G\to G_{\mathrm{ad}}\) induce isomorphisms of the corresponding relative root groups for every \(a\in\Phi(S,G)\); all these root groups may be denoted by \(U_a\).
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a reductive group, and }S\subset G\text{ is a maximal split torus.}

S_{\mathrm{der}}\subset S\text{ is the maximal split torus of }G_{\mathrm{der}};\ S_{\mathrm{sc}}\subset G_{\mathrm{sc}}\text{ is a maximal split torus whose image in }G_{\mathrm{der}}\text{ lies in }S_{\mathrm{der}};\ S_{\mathrm{ad}}\text{ is the image of }S\text{ in }G_{\mathrm{ad}}.
statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi(S_{\mathrm{sc}},G_{\mathrm{sc}})\xrightarrow{\sim}\Phi(S_{\mathrm{der}},G_{\mathrm{der}})\xrightarrow{\sim}\Phi(S,G)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Phi(S_{\mathrm{ad}},G_{\mathrm{ad}}),\quad\text{and for every }a\in\Phi(S,G)\text{ the canonical group maps induce isomorphisms of the corresponding relative root groups.}
statements.scope_note: Comparison of relative root systems and relative root groups under the canonical maps associated with the derived group, simply connected cover, and adjoint quotient of a reductive group.

statements.statement_plain: Assume that the absolute root system of G is of type D4, and let L/K be the splitting extension of the quasi-split group G_K^*. statements.title: Weyl-group equality and positive rescaling to the reduced root system
statements.statement_plain: For a possibly nonreduced root system Phi and its reduced root system ^v Sigma, equality of their Weyl groups is equivalent to the existence, for each root a of Phi, of a positive scalar lambda(a) such that lambda(a)a is a root of ^v Sigma, with the resulting map from Phi onto ^v Sigma surjective.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be a not necessarily reduced root system in the dual of \({}^{v}A\), and let \({}^{v}\!\Sigma\) be its reduced root system. Subgroup orbit patterns on the four non-central vertices give the split D4 folding, the (C2^vee, B2) folding, and the (B3, B3) folding. The extract also records an affine (C1^vee, BC1), finite BC1 folding with Tits index ^2D_{4,1}^{(2)}.

statements.title: Folding of Affine Dynkin Diagrams
statements.statement_plain: Under the specified Gamma-action, form the relative affine Dynkin diagram by taking Gamma-orbits of absolute vertices, inducing edges from links between orbit members, assigning each orbit the gcd-normalized sum of its absolute vertex multiplicities, and declaring an orbit-vertex multipliable exactly when two vertices in that orbit are linked.
statements.statement_latex: Given \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_K\) and its \(\Gamma\)-action via \(\widetilde f\), obtain \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_k\) by orbit-folding with induced edges, gcd-normalized orbit multiplicities, and the stated multipliable-vertex criterion.
assumptions_latex: In the stated connected reductive k-group setting, let \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_K\) be the absolute affine Dynkin diagram, let \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_k\) be the relative affine Dynkin diagram, and let the \(\Gamma\)-action on \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_K\) be given by \(\widetilde f\).
statements.conclusion_latex: Construct \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_k\) as follows: its vertices are the \(\Gamma\)-orbits of vertices of \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_K\); two orbit-vertices are joined exactly when some vertices in the respective orbits are joined in \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_K\); for an orbit-vertex \(v_k\), set \(\widetilde n_{v_k}=\sum_{v\in v_k} n_v\) and set \(n_{v_k}\) equal to \(\widetilde n_{v_k}\) divided by the greatest common divisor of all \(\widetilde n_{v_k}\); finally, \(v_k\) is multipliable exactly when two vertices in its corresponding \(\Gamma\)-orbit are joined in \(\widetilde{\mathcal D}_K\).
statements.scope_note: Folding construction relating absolute and relative affine Dynkin diagrams under the specified Gamma-action.

statements.title: Characterization of k-Pinnings by Relative Root-Group Isomorphisms
statements.statement_plain: For a reductive group over k with B, T, and S as specified, specifying a k-pinning is equivalent to specifying, for every simple relative root, the corresponding restriction-of-scalars isomorphism to its relative root subgroup: the additive form in type R1 and the R2 rank-two form.

assumptions_latex: G is a reductive group over k with Borel subgroup B, maximal k-torus T\subseteq B, and maximal k-split torus S\subseteq T.

\Delta(S,B) denotes the simple relative roots, and for each such root a the required absolute-root lifts in \Delta(T,B) are chosen; in type R2, lifts \widetilde a,\widetilde a' are chosen with \widetilde b=\widetilde a+\widetilde a' also a root.
statements.conclusion_latex: Giving a k-pinning is equivalent to giving, for every simple relative root a\in\Delta(S,B), an isomorphism \operatorname{R}_{k_{\widetilde a}/k}\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_a when a is of type R1, and an isomorphism \operatorname{R}_{k_{\widetilde b}/k}U_{k_{\widetilde a}/k_{\widetilde b}}\xrightarrow{\sim}U_a when a is of type R2.
statements.scope_note: Equivalence between k-pinnings and restriction-of-scalars parametrizations of simple relative root subgroups.

statements.title: Relative Tits-index edge multiplicity and direction
statements.statement_plain: Let a and b be adjacent vertices of the relative Tits-index diagram. Unite their corresponding Theta-orbits with Delta_0, choose a connected component meeting both orbits, and let n_a and n_b be the sums of the coefficients contributed by the two orbit intersections to that component's highest root, with n_a at most n_b. The edge has higher multiplicity exactly when n_a is less than n_b; then n_a equals 1, the multiplicity is n_b, and the edge points toward b.
statements.statement_latex: Let a,b\in\mathcal D_F be vertices joined by an edge, and let O_a,O_b\subset\Delta\setminus\Delta_0 be their corresponding \Theta-orbits. Set \mathcal D'=O_a\cup O_b\cup\Delta_0, and choose a connected component \mathcal D'' of \mathcal D' intersecting both O_a and O_b. Let n_a and n_b be the respective sums of the positive integer coefficients with which the elements of O_a\cap\mathcal D'' and O_b\cap\mathcal D'' occur in the highest root of \mathcal D'', and assume n_a\le n_b. Then the edge between a and b has higher multiplicity if and only if n_a<n_b. In that case n_a=1, the multiplicity is n_b, and the edge points toward b.

statements.title: Root Subgroups and Their Additive Parametrizations
statements.statement_plain: For each root of a split semisimple group, there is a canonical root subgroup normalized by the chosen torus and having the corresponding root space as its Lie algebra. The subgroup is noncanonically isomorphic to the additive group. Its additive parametrizations correspond to nonzero vectors in the root space via the differential at 1, and such a parametrization is defined over k exactly when that vector is k-rational.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a split semisimple group over \(k\), let \(S\) be the chosen torus in the split root-system setup, and put \(\Phi=\Phi(S,G)\subset X^*(S)\). For every \(a\in\Phi\), the root subgroup \(U_a\subset G\) is the canonical subgroup normalized by \(S\) whose Lie algebra is the root space \(\mathfrak g_a\). It is isomorphic, noncanonically, to \(\mathbf G_a\). Choosing an isomorphism \(u_a:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_a\) is equivalent to choosing a nonzero \(X_a\in\mathfrak g_a\), with \(du_a(1)=X_a\); moreover, \(u_a\) is defined over \(k\) if and only if \(X_a\in\mathfrak g_a(k)\).
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a split semisimple algebraic group over }k
S\text{ is the chosen torus defining the split root system}
\Phi=\Phi(S,G)\subset X^*(S)
statements.conclusion_latex: \forall a\in\Phi,\ U_a\subset G\text{ is the canonical subgroup normalized by }S\text{ with }\operatorname{Lie}(U_a)=\mathfrak g_a;\quad U_a\simeq\mathbf G_a\text{ noncanonically};\quad u_a:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_a\ \leftrightarrow\ 0\ne X_a\in\mathfrak g_a\text{ via }du_a(1)=X_a;\quad u_a\text{ is defined over }k\iff X_a\in\mathfrak g_a(k).
statements.scope_note: Definition for roots of a split semisimple group; the additive parametrization is noncanonical and its k-definition is characterized by the corresponding root-space vector.

statements.title: k-Pinnings and Weak Chevalley Systems
statements.statement_plain: Let G be a split semisimple group over k, let S be a maximal split torus, and let B be a Borel subgroup containing S. Choose a nonzero vector X_a in the root space g_a(k) for every simple root a in Delta(S,B). The tuple consisting of S, B, and these vectors is a k-pinning of G; no further conditions are imposed on the vectors. Every such pinning extends to a unique weak Chevalley system and therefore determines a valuation of the root datum.
statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }G\text{ be split semisimple over }k,\ S\subset G\text{ a maximal split torus, and }B\supset S\text{ a Borel subgroup. S\subset G\text{ is a maximal split torus}
B\subset G\text{ is a Borel subgroup containing }S

statements.title: Weak Chevalley Systems, Chevalley Systems, and the Tits Group
statements.statement_plain: A weak Chevalley system chooses, for each root a, a pair of nonzero elements plus or minus X_a in the root space g_a(k_s), and each w(X_a) preserves the entire signed family. A Chevalley system (or Chevalley basis) chooses X_a for each root, requires [X_a,X_-a] = H_a, and requires its signed family to be weak Chevalley; it refines the weak system. The subgroup of N_G(T)(k) generated by all w(X_a) is called the Tits group.
statements.statement_latex: (1) A weak Chevalley system is a set X_{\mathrm{weak}}=\{\pm X_a\mid a\in\Phi\}, containing for each a\in\Phi a pair of nonzero elements \pm X_a\in\mathfrak g_a(k_s), such that X_{\mathrm{weak}} is preserved by w(X_a) for each a\in\Phi. (2) A Chevalley system (or Chevalley basis) is a set X=\{X_a\mid a\in\Phi\} with [X_a,X_{-a}]=H_a and with signed family \{\pm X_a\mid a\in\Phi\} a weak Chevalley system; X is said to refine X_{\mathrm{weak}}. (3) Given a weak Chevalley system, the subgroup \dot W\subset N_G(T)(k) generated by w(X_a) for all a\in\Phi is called the Tits group.
assumptions_latex: \Phi\text{ is the root system under consideration.}
X_a\in\mathfrak g_a(k_s)\text{ is nonzero for each }a\in\Phi.
w(X_a)\text{ denotes the element used in the source to act on the signed family.}
statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A weak Chevalley system is }X_{\mathrm{weak}}=\{\pm X_a\mid a\in\Phi\}\text{ preserved by }w(X_a)\text{ for every }a\in\Phi;\ \text{a Chevalley system }X=\{X_a\mid a\in\Phi\}\text{ satisfies }[X_a,X_{-a}]=H_a\text{ and has signed family }\{\pm X_a\mid a\in\Phi\}\text{ weak Chevalley (so }X\text{ refines }X_{\mathrm{weak}}\text{); given a weak system, }\dot W=\langle w(X_a)\mid a\in\Phi\rangle\subset N_G(T)(k)\text{ is the Tits group}.

statements.title: Simply Connected Cover Convention for Chevalley Systems
statements.statement_plain: For a connected reductive quasi-split k-group G, let G_sc be the simply connected cover of its derived subgroup. By convention, a weak or ordinary Chevalley or Chevalley-Steinberg system for G is one for G_sc. Passing to this cover does not change the root groups, so root-group structure results and commutation relations remain valid for G.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected reductive quasi-split \(k\)-group, and let \(G_{\mathrm{sc}}\) be the simply connected cover of \(G_{\mathrm{der}}\). A (weak) Chevalley system or (weak) Chevalley-Steinberg system for \(G\) means such a system for \(G_{\mathrm{sc}}\). Passing from \(G\) to \(G_{\mathrm{sc}}\) does not change the root groups, so results about their structure and their commutation relations remain valid for \(G\).
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected reductive quasi-split }k\text{-group}

statements.title: Basis-induced pinning of GL and SL
statements.statement_plain: For GL(X) or SL(X), a chosen basis gives the diagonal maximal torus, the corresponding flag Borel subgroup, and standard additive parametrizations of all simple root subgroups, hence a pinning.
statements.statement_latex: For G=\mathrm{GL}(X) or \mathrm{SL}(X) with basis (v_1,\ldots,v_n), the stabilizer of the basis-line decomposition is a maximal torus, the stabilizer of the associated complete flag is a Borel subgroup containing that torus, and the elementary \mathbf G_a-morphisms x\mapsto(v_{i+1}\mapsto xv_i+v_{i+1},\ v_j\mapsto v_j\ (j\ne i+1)) parametrize the simple root subgroups; therefore the basis yields a pinning.
assumptions_latex: G=\mathrm{GL}(X) or G=\mathrm{SL}(X), where (v_1,\ldots,v_n) is a basis of X
l_i=\langle v_i\rangle and X_i=l_1\oplus\cdots\oplus l_i
statements.conclusion_latex: The stabilizer T of the decomposition X=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n l_i is a maximal torus of G; the stabilizer B of the flag X_1\subset X_2\subset\cdots\subset X_n is a Borel subgroup containing T; for 1\le i<n, the morphism \mathbf G_a\to G sending x to the linear map v_{i+1}\mapsto xv_i+v_{i+1} and fixing v_j for j\ne i+1 parametrizes the corresponding simple root subgroup. Hence the basis determines a pinning of G.
statements.scope_note: Basis-induced standard pinning data for the algebraic groups GL(X) and SL(X).

statements.title: Chevalley commutator constants
statements.statement_plain: In the split case, a fixed Chevalley system has integer constants giving the commutator of two non-opposite root elements as an ordered product over all roots ia+jb in the root system, with parameters C_{a,b;i,j}u^iv^j. Defining M_{a,b,i}=C_{a,b;i,1} where that constant is indexed, and M_{a,b,0}=I, the defined M_{a,b,i} equal ±I whenever a−b is not a root.
statements.statement_latex: For a fixed Chevalley system \((x_a)_{a\in\Phi}\) in the split case, for \(a,b\in\Phi\) with \(b\neq -a\), there are integers \(C_{a,b;i,j}\), indexed by \(i,j\in\mathbf N^{*}\) with \(ia+jb\in\Phi\), such that the commutator formula \(\left(x_a(u),x_b(v)\right)=\prod x_{ia+jb}(C_{a,b;i,j}u^iv^j)\) holds, with the involved roots in any prescribed order. Setting \(M_{a,b,i}=C_{a,b;i,1}\) (for \(ia+b\in\Phi\)) and \(M_{a,b,0}=I\), if \(a-b\notin\Phi\) then \(M_{a,b,i}=\pm I\).
assumptions_latex: A fixed Chevalley system \((x_a)_{a\in\Phi}\) is used in the split-case setting.
\(a,b\in\Phi\) with \(b\neq -a\); the indices \(i,j\in\mathbf N^{*}\) range over those satisfying \(ia+jb\in\Phi\).
statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \left(x_a(u),x_b(v)\right)=\prod_{\substack{i,j\in\mathbf N^{*}\\ ia+jb\in\Phi}}x_{ia+jb}\!\left(C_{a,b;i,j}u^{i}v^{j}\right)\), with the roots \(ia+jb\) in any prescribed order. Defining \(M_{a,b,i}=C_{a,b;i,1}\) when \(ia+b\in\Phi\) and \(M_{a,b,0}=I\), one has \(M_{a,b,i}=\pm I\) whenever \(a-b\notin\Phi\).\)

statements.title: Commutation formulas for 135-degree short-long roots
statements.statement_plain: In the 135-degree case where a is short and b is long, V_a is the restriction of scalars from ell to k of the additive root group over ell, while V_b is the additive root group over k. The possible roots are a+b (short, with the same restriction-of-scalars root group) and 2a+b (long, with the k-root group), and the corresponding commutation coordinates satisfy gamma for a+b equivalent to uv and gamma for 2a+b equivalent to the norm of u from ell to k times v.

If c=a+b is short with V_c=\mathrm{R}_{\ell/k}\mathbf{G}_{a,\ell}, or c=2a+b is long with V_c=\mathbf{G}_{a,k}, then \gamma_{a,b}^{a+b}(u,v)\sim uv and \gamma_{a,b}^{2a+b}(u,v)\sim \mathrm{N}_{\ell/k}(u)\,v.

statements.title: Structure of a Multipliable Relative Root Subgroup
statements.statement_plain: For a multipliable relative root a, two nonorthogonal absolute roots above a sum to the absolute root above 2a. Their associated field extension is quadratic Galois. The product of the three corresponding absolute root subgroups is a connected three-dimensional noncommutative unipotent group over the smaller field, and its restriction of scalars is the relative root subgroup U_a. On rational points the isomorphism is the product over the relevant Galois cosets. Distinct geometric copies commute, so noncommutativity occurs only within each copy.
statements.statement_latex: Let a be a relative root with U_{2a}\subset U_a. Choose \widetilde a\in\widetilde\Phi above a, let \widetilde a' be the unique other nonorthogonal root above a, and put \widetilde b=\widetilde a+\widetilde a', which lies above 2a. Then F_{\widetilde a}/F_{\widetilde b} is Galois of degree two, with nontrivial automorphism induced by the unique element of \Theta interchanging \widetilde a and \widetilde a'. The product U_{[\widetilde a]}:=U_{\widetilde a}U_{\widetilde a'}U_{\widetilde b} is a connected three-dimensional unipotent F_{\widetilde b}-subgroup of G, noncanonically isomorphic to U_{F_{\widetilde a}/F_{\widetilde b}} and noncommutative. There is an isomorphism of algebraic F-groups \operatorname{R}_{F_{\widetilde b}/F}U_{[\widetilde a]}\xrightarrow{\sim}U_a, hence an abstract-group isomorphism U_{[\widetilde a]}(F_{\widetilde b})\xrightarrow{\sim}U_a(F) sending u to \prod_{\sigma\in\Theta/\Theta_{\widetilde b}}\sigma(u). After base change to F_s, the distinct copies of U_{[\widetilde a]} in U_a\times_FF_s\simeq\left(U_{[\widetilde a]}\right)^{[F_{\widetilde b}:F]} commute with one another.

\widetilde a\in\widetilde\Phi\text{ maps to }a,\text{ and }\widetilde a'\text{ is the unique other root mapping to }a\text{ that is not orthogonal to }\widetilde a.

statements.title: Chevalley commutator formula for split groups
statements.statement_plain: For a split group G with T=S, the commutator of root elements u_a(x_a) and u_b(x_b) factors as a product of root elements indexed by positive combinations pa+qb that are roots, with parameters ±c_{p,q}x_a^p x_b^q and coefficients c_{p,q} equal to 1, 2, or 3.

For split G with T=S, the Chevalley commutator of root elements satisfies
\[
u_a(x_a)u_b(x_b)u_a(x_a)^{-1}u_b(x_b)^{-1}=\prod_{\substack{p,q\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}\\pa+qb\in\bar\Phi}}u_{pa+qb}\!\left(\pm c_{p,q}x_a^p x_b^q\right),
\]
where each c_{p,q} is an integer equal to 1, 2, or 3.

statements.title: Chevalley involution of a pinning
statements.statement_plain: For a pinned group (G,B,T,{X_a}), with each opposite root vector X_{-a} uniquely normalized by [X_a,X_{-a}] = d a^vee(1) in Lie(G_sc), there is a unique automorphism of G that preserves T, sends every t in T to t^{-1}, and maps each pinned root vector X_a to -X_{-a}. It is called the Chevalley involution of the pinning.

Then there exists a unique automorphism \theta of G preserving T, acting by inversion on T, and sending X_{\widetilde a} to -X_{-\widetilde a} for every simple root \widetilde a. This automorphism is the Chevalley involution of the pinning.

statements.title: Properties of Chevalley Root-Group Valuations
statements.statement_plain: The root-group valuation maps determined by a Chevalley system depend only on its weak Chevalley system. Their nontrivial images are Z-torsors; their level sets are bounded open root-group subgroups with trivial infinite level; torus conjugation shifts valuation by the root character valuation; and Tits-group conjugation is equivariant under the Weyl-group action.

For each root \(a\), the maps \(\varphi_{o+v,a}\) satisfy: (i) the collection depends only on the underlying weak Chevalley system; (ii) \(\varphi_{o+v,a}(U_a(k)\setminus\{1\})\) is a \(\mathbf Z\)-torsor in \(\mathbf R\); (iii) for every \(r\in\mathbf R\), \(U_{a,r}:=\varphi_{o+v,a}^{-1}([r,\infty))\) is a bounded open subgroup of \(U_a(k)\), while \(U_{a,\infty}:=\varphi_{o+v,a}^{-1}(\infty)=\{1\}\); (iv) for \(t\in S_{\mathrm{ad}}(k)\) and \(u\in U_a(k)\), \(\varphi_{o+v,a}(tut^{-1})=\varphi_{o+v,a}(u)+\omega(a(t))\); and (v) if \(n\in\dot W\subset N_G(S')(k)\) maps to \(w\in W\), then \(\varphi_{o+wv,wa}(nun^{-1})=\varphi_{o+v,a}(u)\).
assumptions_latex: The source is working in the split semisimple Chevalley-system setting.
\(o\) is a Chevalley system with underlying weak Chevalley system, and \(v\) is the parameter occurring in \(\varphi_{o+v,a}\).

statements.conclusion_latex: (1) \(\{\varphi_{o+v,a}\}_a\) depends only on the underlying weak Chevalley system. (2) \(\varphi_{o+v,a}(U_a(k)\setminus\{1\})\) is a \(\mathbf Z\)-torsor. (3) \(U_{a,r}=\varphi_{o+v,a}^{-1}([r,\infty))\) is bounded and open in \(U_a(k)\), and \(U_{a,\infty}=\{1\}\). (4) \(\varphi_{o+v,a}(tut^{-1})=\varphi_{o+v,a}(u)+\omega(a(t))\). statements.title: Open Product Decomposition for Closed Root Subsets

In particular, \(\mathrm{U}_{\Phi^{-}}\times\mathrm{Z}\times\mathrm{U}_{\Phi^{+}}\) identifies via multiplication with an open neighborhood of the identity in \(\mathrm{G}\), equal to \(\mathrm{G}\) when \(\mathrm{G}\) is solvable.

statements.title: Valuation homomorphisms from a maximal K-split subtorus
statements.statement_plain: Let S be the maximal K-split subtorus of the K-torus T. Restriction injects the K-rational characters of T into the characters of S with finite cokernel, so their rational character spaces are canonically the same. Using that identification, every rational character c gives the valuation homomorphism omega composed with c from T(K) to R.
statements.statement_latex: For a K-torus T with maximal K-split subtorus S, restriction X_K^*(T)\hookrightarrow X^*(S) is injective with finite cokernel. Thus the rational character spaces are canonically identified, and this identification defines \omega\circ c:T(K)\to\mathbf{R} for every c\in X^*(S)\otimes\mathbf{Q}, as in §4.2.5.
assumptions_latex: T is a K-torus and S\hookrightarrow T is its maximal K-split subtorus.
\omega is the valuation map used in §4.2.5.
statements.conclusion_latex: The restriction homomorphism X_K^*(T)\to X^*(S) is injective with finite cokernel, hence X^*(S)\otimes\mathbf{Q}\cong X_K^*(T)\otimes\mathbf{Q} canonically; via this identification, for every c\in X^*(S)\otimes\mathbf{Q}, the homomorphism \omega\circ c:T(K)\to\mathbf{R} is defined as in §4.2.5.
statements.scope_note: Character-group construction of valuation homomorphisms on the K-points of a torus using its maximal K-split subtorus.

statements.title: Boundedness and compactness criteria for anisotropic reductive groups
statements.statement_plain: For a reductive group G over the valued field k, G(k) is bounded exactly when G is anisotropic over k. If k is locally compact and nondiscrete, G(k) is compact exactly when G is k-anisotropic.

k\text{ is locally compact with nondiscrete topology for the compactness equivalence}.
statements.conclusion_latex: G(k)\text{ is bounded}\iff G\text{ is anisotropic over }k;\quad \text{if }k\text{ is locally compact and nondiscrete, then }G(k)\text{ is compact}\iff G\text{ is }k\text{-anisotropic}.

statements.title: Characterization and functoriality of the bounded subgroup of a torus
statements.statement_plain: For a torus T over the valued field K that splits over the indicated extension, the bounded subgroup consists exactly of elements on which every character has valuation zero. It equals the intersection of the bounded subgroup over the splitting field with T(K), is the largest bounded subgroup of T(K), is carried into the bounded subgroup of any target torus split over the same extension by a K-group morphism, and contains the integral points of every flat group scheme over the valuation ring with generic fibre T.
statements.statement_latex:
Let (K,\omega) be a valued field with valuation ring \mathcal O, and let T be a K-torus split over \widetilde K. Then
\[
T_b(K)=\{t\in T(K):\omega(\chi(t))=0\text{ for all }\chi\in X^*_{\widetilde K}(T)=X^*(T)\}=T_b(\widetilde K)\cap T(K),
\]
and T_b(K) is the largest bounded subgroup of T(K) for the natural bornology induced by \omega. If u:T\to T' is a K-group morphism to a K-torus T' split over \widetilde K, then u(T_b(K))\subseteq T'_b(K). If \mathfrak T is a flat \mathcal O-group scheme with generic fibre T, then \mathfrak T(\mathcal O)\subseteq T_b(K).
assumptions_latex: (K,\omega)\text{ is a valued field with valuation ring }\mathcal O.
T\text{ is a }K\text{-torus split over }\widetilde K.
u:T\to T'\text{ is a }K\text{-group morphism, where }T'\text{ is a }K\text{-torus split over }\widetilde K.
\mathfrak T\text{ is a flat }\mathcal O\text{-group scheme with generic fibre }T.
statements.conclusion_latex: T_b(K)=\{t\in T(K):\omega(\chi(t))=0\text{ for every }\chi\in X^*_{\widetilde K}(T)=X^*(T)\}=T_b(\widetilde K)\cap T(K),\quad T_b(K)\text{ is the largest bounded subgroup of }T(K)\text{ for the natural bornology induced by }\omega;\quad u(T_b(K))\subseteq T'_b(K),\quad \mathfrak T(\mathcal O)\subseteq T_b(K).
statements.scope_note: Boundedness is with respect to the natural bornology on T(K) induced by the valuation.

statements.title: Conjugacy classes of maximal bounded subgroups for cyclic Xi
statements.statement_plain: When Xi is cyclic of order q, the number c of conjugacy classes of maximal bounded subgroups of G is less than ell plus 1 for q greater than 2, and equals ell plus 1 for q equal to 1 or 2. If Xi cyclically permutes a subset Y of the affine simple-root set, the maximal bounded subgroups Stab B_X with X containing the complement of Y give as many conjugacy classes as Y has positive divisors.
statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\Xi\) is cyclic of order \(q\), \(\ell=\dim A\), and \(c\) is the number of conjugacy classes of maximal bounded subgroups of \(G\). Then \(c<\ell+1\) when \(q>2\), while \(c=\ell+1\) when \(q=1\) or \(q=2\). Moreover, if \(\Xi\) cyclically permutes a subset \(Y\subseteq\mathbf S\), the number of conjugacy classes of maximal bounded subgroups of the form \(\operatorname{Stab} B_X\) with \(X\supset \mathbf S\setminus Y\) equals the number of positive divisors of \(|Y|\).
assumptions_latex: \(\Xi\) is cyclic of order \(q\) and acts on the affine simple-root set \(\mathbf S\) in the preceding setup.
\(\ell=\dim A\), where \(A\) is the apartment.
\(Y\subseteq\mathbf S\) is a subset cyclically permuted by \(\Xi\); consider maximal bounded subgroups \(\operatorname{Stab} B_X\) with \(X\supset \mathbf S\setminus Y\).
statements.conclusion_latex: The number \(c\) of conjugacy classes of maximal bounded subgroups of \(G\) satisfies \(c<\ell+1\) for \(q>2\), and \(c=\ell+1\) for \(q=1\) or \(q=2\). For such a cyclically permuted subset \(Y\), the number of conjugacy classes of maximal bounded subgroups of the form \(\operatorname{Stab} B_X\) with \(X\supset \mathbf S\setminus Y\) equals the number of positive divisors of \(|Y|\).
statements.scope_note: Counts conjugacy classes of maximal bounded subgroups under a cyclic \(\Xi\)-action, including the global bound and equality cases and the divisor count for each cyclically permuted subset of affine simple roots.

statements.title: Functoriality of bounded subgroups of tori
statements.statement_plain: A morphism of k-tori maps the bounded subgroup of the source into the bounded subgroup of the target. If its kernel is anisotropic, in particular if it is finite, the source bounded subgroup is exactly the inverse image of the target bounded subgroup.

assumptions_latex: f:T\to T'\text{ is a morphism of }k\text{-tori}
statements.conclusion_latex: f\bigl(T(k)_b\bigr)\subseteq T'(k)_b;\qquad \ker(f)\text{ anisotropic }\Longrightarrow T(k)_b=f^{-1}\bigl(T'(k)_b\bigr).
statements.scope_note: The inverse-image equality requires the kernel to be anisotropic; a finite kernel is an explicitly stated sufficient special case. The notation T(k)_b and T'(k)_b denotes the respective bounded subgroups used in the source.

statements.title: Maximal bounded subgroup containment and irreducible alternative
statements.statement_plain: Let x lie in the apartment A and let D be a vector chamber. Every bounded subgroup of G containing B_{x,D} is contained in \widehat{P}_x. If the root system Phi is irreducible, every subgroup of bold G containing bold B_{x,D} is either contained in \widehat{bold P}_x or else contains G', the subgroup of G generated by H and all root groups U_a for a in Phi.

(i) Every bounded subgroup of }\mathrm{G}\text{ containing }\mathrm{B}_{x,\mathrm{D}}\text{ is contained in }\widehat{\mathrm{P}}_{x}.\text{ (ii) If }\Phi\text{ is irreducible, every subgroup of }\mathbf{G}\text{ containing }\mathbf{B}_{x,\mathrm{D}}\text{ is either contained in }\widehat{\mathbf{P}}_{x}\text{ or else contains the subgroup }\mathrm{G}'\text{ of }\mathrm{G}\text{ generated by }\mathrm{H}\text{ and the }\mathrm{U}_{a}\ (a\in\Phi).

statements.title: Maximal bounded subgroups, pro-p overgroups, and lattice stabilizers
statements.statement_plain: Let 𝒢 be an open subgroup of G(k). Every bounded subgroup of 𝒢 is contained in a maximal bounded open subgroup of 𝒢. If k is complete, has finite residue field, and has characteristic p, every pro-p subgroup of 𝒢 is contained in a maximal open pro-p subgroup. For a finite-dimensional k-vector space V, a subgroup B of GL(V) is maximal bounded exactly when it is the stabilizer GL(Λ) of a lattice Λ in V.
statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }\mathcal G\text{ be an open subgroup of }G(k).\ \text{Then every bounded subgroup of }\mathcal G\text{ is contained in a maximal bounded open subgroup of }\mathcal G.\ \text{If }k\text{ is complete with finite residue field and }\operatorname{char}(k)=p,\text{ every pro-}p\text{ subgroup of }\mathcal G\text{ is contained in a maximal open pro-}p\text{ subgroup.}\ \text{For a finite-dimensional }k\text{-vector space }V,\text{ a subgroup }B\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)\text{ is maximal bounded if and only if }B=\operatorname{GL}(\Lambda)\text{ for some lattice }\Lambda\subset V.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal G\leq G(k)\text{ is an open subgroup}
\text{For (2), }k\text{ is complete, its residue field is finite, and }\operatorname{char}(k)=p
\text{For (3), }V\text{ is a finite-dimensional }k\text{-vector space}
statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{(1) Every bounded subgroup of }\mathcal G\text{ is contained in a maximal bounded open subgroup of }\mathcal G.\\&\text{(2) Every pro-}p\text{ subgroup of }\mathcal G\text{ is contained in a maximal open pro-}p\text{ subgroup of }\mathcal G.\\&\text{(3) For finite-dimensional }V,\ B\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)\text{ is maximal bounded if and only if }B=\operatorname{GL}(\Lambda)\text{ for some lattice }\Lambda\subset V.\end{aligned}
statements.scope_note: Clause (1) concerns bounded subgroups of the open subgroup \(\mathcal G\); clause (2) adds completeness, finite residue field, and characteristic \(p\) hypotheses; clause (3) is the characterization for the linear group \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\) via lattice stabilizers.

statements.title: Unique maximal bounded subgroup of a torus
statements.statement_plain: Let k be a discretely valued Henselian field with perfect residue field, let K be the maximal unramified extension of k in a fixed separable closure, and let T be a k-torus. Then T(k) has a unique maximal bounded subgroup, denoted T(k)_b or T(k)^1. It is the kernel of the torus valuation homomorphism and equals the elements on which every Theta-invariant character, equivalently every character as stated in the source, has valuation zero. Moreover, T(k) is bounded if and only if T is anisotropic, equivalently when the Theta-invariant character group is zero.
statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k\) be a discretely valued Henselian field with perfect residue field, let \(K\) be the maximal unramified extension in a fixed separable closure \(k_s\), and let \(T\) be a \(k\)-torus. Then \(T(k)\) has a unique maximal bounded subgroup, denoted \(T(k)_b\) or \(T(k)^1\), and
\[
T(k)_b=\ker(\omega_T)=\{x\in T(k)\mid \forall\chi\in X^*(T)^\Theta,\ \omega(\chi(x))=0\}=\{x\in T(k)\mid \forall\chi\in X^*(T),\ \omega(\chi(x))=0\}.
\]
In particular, \(T(k)\) is bounded if and only if \(T\) is anisotropic, equivalently \(X^*(T)^\Theta=\{0\}\).
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is a discretely valued Henselian field with perfect residue field}
K\text{ is the maximal unramified extension of }k\text{ in a fixed separable closure }k_s
T\text{ is a }k\text{-torus}
statements.conclusion_latex: T(k)_b=T(k)^1=\ker(\omega_T)=\{x\in T(k)\mid \forall\chi\in X^*(T)^\Theta,\ \omega(\chi(x))=0\}=\{x\in T(k)\mid \forall\chi\in X^*(T),\ \omega(\chi(x))=0\},\quad T(k)\text{ is bounded}\Longleftrightarrow T\text{ is anisotropic}\Longleftrightarrow X^*(T)^\Theta=\{0\}.
statements.scope_note: Retain the source-local notation \(\omega_T\), \(\omega\), and \(\Theta\); \(K\) is the maximal unramified extension specified in the preceding context.

statements.title: Definition of G(k)^0
statements.statement_plain: Let G be a connected reductive group with center Z(G). Define G(k)^0 as follows: if G is quasi-split, choose a maximally split maximal torus T and set G(k)^0 = G(k)^natural times T(k)^0; if G/Z(G) is anisotropic, set G(k)^0 = G(K)^0 intersected with G(k), where G(K)^0 is defined by the quasi-split case because G_K is quasi-split; for general G, choose a minimal Levi subgroup M_0 and set G(k)^0 = G(k)^natural times M_0(k)^0.
statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }G\text{ be a connected reductive group with center }Z(G).\text{ Define }G(k)^0\subset G(k)\text{ by}\quad G(k)^0=\begin{cases}G(k)^\natural\,T(k)^0,&\text{if }G\text{ is quasi-split, for a chosen maximally split maximal torus }T\subset G,\\ G(K)^0\cap G(k),&\text{if }G/Z(G)\text{ is anisotropic, where }G(K)^0\text{ is defined by the quasi-split case since }G_K\text{ is quasi-split},\\ G(k)^\natural\,{M_0}(k)^0,&\text{for general }G,\text{ after choosing a minimal Levi subgroup }M_0\subset G.\end{cases}
assumptions_latex: G is a connected reductive group with center Z(G).
In the quasi-split case, T is a chosen maximally split maximal torus of G.
In the anisotropic-central-quotient case, G/Z(G) is anisotropic and G_K is quasi-split.
In the general case, M_0 is a chosen minimal Levi subgroup of G.
statements.conclusion_latex: G(k)^0\subset G(k) is defined by the three displayed cases.
statements.scope_note: For a connected reductive group G, define the subgroup G(k)^0 according to whether G is quasi-split, has anisotropic central quotient, or is general.

statements.title: Levi central-torus cocharacter decomposition
statements.statement_plain: For a Levi subgroup M of G, let A_G and A_M be the maximal split central tori of G and M, and let A_M' be the maximal torus in A_M intersected with the derived group of G. The composite map from A_M' to A_M/A_G is an isogeny, so it is an isomorphism on rational cocharacter spaces. This gives a canonical splitting and decomposes the rational cocharacter space of A_M as the direct sum of those of A_G and A_M'.
statements.statement_latex: Let M\subset G be a Levi subgroup, with A_G and A_M the maximal split tori in the centers of G and M, and let A_M' be the maximal torus in A_M\cap G_{\mathrm{der}}. Then A_M'\to A_M\to A_M/A_G is an isogeny. It induces an isomorphism \(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M')\cong\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M/A_G)\), yielding a canonical splitting and the direct-sum decomposition \(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M)=\bigl(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_G)\bigr)\oplus\bigl(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M')\bigr).
assumptions_latex: M\subset G\text{ is a Levi subgroup}
A_G\text{ and }A_M\text{ are the maximal split tori in the centers of }G\text{ and }M\text{, respectively}
A_M'\text{ is the maximal torus in }A_M\cap G_{\mathrm{der}}
statements.conclusion_latex: The composite A_M'\to A_M\to A_M/A_G is an isogeny, inducing an isomorphism \(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M')\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M/A_G)\). Consequently, the induced inclusion gives a canonical splitting \(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M)=\bigl(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_G)\bigr)\oplus\bigl(\mathbf Q\otimes_{\mathbf Z}X_*(A_M')\bigr).
statements.scope_note: Structural statement for maximal split central tori of a Levi subgroup and their rational cocharacter spaces.

statements.title: Affine root-group filtration and product decomposition
statements.statement_plain: Let psi be an affine root in Psi-prime with derivative a in Phi. If 2a is not a root, then psi is in Psi. If psi is not in Psi, then 2psi is in Psi and there is a larger affine root psi-prime in Psi. For the smallest psi-prime in Psi satisfying psi-prime at least psi, the root subgroup satisfies U_psi = U_psi-prime times U_2psi.
statements.statement_latex: Let \(\psi\in\Psi'\) have derivative \(a\in\Phi\). (1) If \(2a\notin\Phi\), then \(\psi\in\Psi\). (3) If \(\psi'\in\Psi\) is the smallest affine root with \(\psi'\geq\psi\), then \(U_\psi=U_{\psi'}\cdot U_{2\psi}\).

statements.title: Faithful Linear Representations of Affine Group Schemes
statements.statement_plain: A representation of an affine group scheme is faithful precisely when its morphism to the general linear group is a closed immersion, equivalently when its matrix coefficients and inverse determinant generate the coordinate algebra. Every flat affine group scheme of finite type over a Dedekind ring admits a faithful representation on a finitely generated projective module.
statements.statement_latex: A representation \(\rho:\mathfrak X\to\mathfrak{GL}(M)\) is faithful exactly when it is a closed immersion, equivalently when the coefficients \(c^{\circ}_{m',m}\) and \((\det\rho)^{-1}\) generate \(A[\mathfrak X]\). If \(A\) is Dedekind and \(\mathfrak X\) is a flat affine group scheme of finite type over \(A\), then \(\mathfrak X\) has a faithful representation on a finitely generated projective \(A\)-module.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a commutative ring, \(\mathfrak X\) is an affine group scheme over \(A\), and \(\rho:\mathfrak X\to\mathfrak{GL}(M)\) is a representation.
For the existence assertion, \(A\) is a Dedekind ring and \(\mathfrak X\) is flat, affine, and of finite type over \(A\).
statements.conclusion_latex: The representation \(\rho\) is faithful (equivalently, a closed immersion) if and only if the coefficients \(c^{\circ}_{m',m}\) of \(\rho\), together with \((\det\rho)^{-1}\), generate the coordinate algebra \(A[\mathfrak X]\). Under the Dedekind hypotheses, \(\mathfrak X\) admits a faithful representation on a finitely generated projective \(A\)-module.
statements.scope_note: Faithful representations of affine group schemes, their coordinate-algebra criterion, and their existence over Dedekind bases.

statements.title: Affine functions on finite products of affine spaces
statements.statement_plain: For affine spaces over a common field, affine functions on a finite product are obtained by summing pullbacks of affine functions from the factors. For two factors each pullback is injective and characterized by derivatives supported on that factor; the sum map is exact with anti-diagonal constant kernel. For n factors the kernel consists of constant tuples whose entries sum to zero.
statements.statement_latex: Let A_1,A_2 be affine spaces over k-vector spaces V_1,V_2 and let A=A_1\times A_2 over V=V_1\times V_2. Pullback along each projection A\to A_i gives an injection A_i^*\hookrightarrow A^*; its image is exactly the affine functions whose derivative lies in the embedded V_i^*\subset V^*. The sum map A_1^*\oplus A_2^*\to A^* is surjective and has anti-diagonal constant kernel, yielding the exact sequence 0\to k\to A_1^*\oplus A_2^*\to A^*\to0. More generally, for finite A=\prod_{i=1}^n A_i, the summation map \bigoplus_i A_i^*\to A^* is surjective with kernel the constant tuples (c_i) satisfying \sum_i c_i=0.
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is the base field of the affine spaces and affine function spaces.}

statements.title: Affine Functionals and Affine Hyperplanes
statements.statement_plain: Affine functionals on A form a k-vector space. Taking the linear part gives a surjective linear map to V*, whose kernel is exactly the constant functionals, identified with k, yielding an exact sequence. One-dimensional subspaces of A* other than the constant line correspond bijectively to affine hyperplanes via the zero set of any nonzero representative.

Moreover, \psi\mapsto H_\psi, where H_\psi=\{a\in A\mid\psi(a)=0\}, induces a bijection between the one-dimensional subspaces of A^* other than the constant line and the affine hyperplanes of A.

statements.title: Affine functionals and hyperplanes containing a subset
statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty subset Omega of an affine space A, an affine functional vanishes on Omega exactly when it vanishes on the affine span of Omega. If W is the derivative space of that span, taking derivatives gives an isomorphism from the affine functionals vanishing on Omega to the annihilator of W. Therefore affine hyperplanes containing Omega correspond bijectively to lines in either vector space.

assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an affine space over }k\text{ with translation space }V.
\varnothing\neq\Omega\subset A.
W\subset V\text{ is the derivative space of the affine span }\langle\Omega\rangle.
statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{(1) }\psi|_{\Omega}=0\iff\psi|_{\langle\Omega\rangle}=0.\\&\text{(2) }\nabla:A_{\Omega}^{*}\xrightarrow{\sim}W^{\perp}.\\&\text{(3) Affine hyperplanes in }A\text{ containing }\Omega\text{ correspond bijectively to lines in }A_{\Omega}^{*},\text{ and hence to lines in }W^{\perp}.\end{aligned}
statements.scope_note: A_{\Omega}^{*} is the vector space of affine functionals on A vanishing on \Omega; \nabla denotes the derivative (linear part), and W^{\perp}\subset V^{*} is the annihilator of W. The correspondence in (3) sends a hyperplane H_{\psi} to the one-dimensional subspace k^{\times}\!\cdot\psi.

statements.title: Chambers, faces, and parahoric facet incidence
statements.statement_plain: If P is contained in the parahoric subgroup Q of G(K), then the facet F_Q is contained in its closure and that closure is contained in F_P, so F_Q is a face of F_P. F_P is maximal exactly when P is a minimal parahoric subgroup. Maximal facets of the Bruhat–Tits building are called chambers and all chambers have equal dimension. A facet F' is a face of F exactly when F' is contained in the closure of F.
statements.statement_latex: For parahoric subgroups P\subseteq Q of G(K), one has \mathcal F_Q\subseteq\overline{\mathcal F}_Q\subseteq\mathcal F_P and hence \mathcal F_Q\prec\mathcal F_P. Consequently, \mathcal F_P is a maximal facet exactly when P is a minimal parahoric subgroup. The maximal facets of \mathfrak B are called chambers (all chambers have the same dimension). A facet \mathcal F' is a face of a facet \mathcal F exactly when \mathcal F'\prec\mathcal F, equivalently when \mathcal F' is contained in the closure of \mathcal F.
assumptions_latex: P,Q\leq G(K) are parahoric subgroups with P\subseteq Q.
statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F_Q\subseteq\overline{\mathcal F}_Q\subseteq\mathcal F_P,\quad \mathcal F_Q\prec\mathcal F_P;\quad \mathcal F_P\text{ is maximal if and only if }P\text{ is a minimal parahoric subgroup}.\text{ The maximal facets of }\mathfrak B\text{ are called chambers, all chambers have equal dimension, and }\mathcal F'\text{ is a face of }\mathcal F\text{ if and only if }\mathcal F'\prec\mathcal F\text{ (equivalently, }\mathcal F'\subseteq\overline{\mathcal F}\text{).}
statements.scope_note: Facet, chamber, and face incidence in the Bruhat–Tits building \mathfrak B of G(K), together with its parahoric-containment characterization.

statements.title: Chambers, Walls, Galleries, and Taut Galleries
statements.statement_plain: Assuming the facet dimensions of A are bounded above, codimension is the dimension of A minus facet dimension. Codimension-zero facets are chambers and codimension-one facets are walls; chambers are adjacent when distinct and sharing a wall. Galleries are chamber sequences with consecutive chambers adjacent or equal, with defined origins, extremities, and without-stammering condition. Connection and shortest (taut) galleries between facets or points, and minimal galleries, are defined accordingly.
statements.statement_latex: Assume the dimensions of the facets of A are bounded above and set dim A = sup{dim F : F in the facet set of A}. For each facet F, define codim F = dim A - dim F. Codimension-zero facets are chambers and codimension-one facets are walls; distinct chambers sharing a wall are adjacent. A gallery of length n is Gamma = (C_0,...,C_n) with n+1 chambers and each consecutive pair adjacent or coincident. Its origin and extremity are C_0 and C_n, and it is without stammering iff C_{i-1} != C_i for 1 <= i <= n. It connects facets F and F' iff F is contained in the closure of C_0 and F' in the closure of C_n; it is taut between them iff no shorter connecting gallery exists. Tautness between points is induced by their containing facets, and a minimal gallery is one taut between its extremities.
assumptions_latex: The dimensions of the facets of A are bounded above, and dim A denotes their supremum.
statements.conclusion_latex: For F in the facet set of A, codim F = dim A - dim F; facets of codimension 0 are chambers and facets of codimension 1 are walls. Distinct chambers sharing a common wall are adjacent. A gallery of length n is a sequence Gamma = (C_0,...,C_n) of n+1 chambers such that each consecutive pair is adjacent or coincident; C_0 and C_n are its origin and extremity, and the gallery is without stammering when C_{i-1} != C_i for every 1 <= i <= n. A gallery connects facets F and F' when F is contained in the closure of C_0 and F' in the closure of C_n; it is taut between them when no shorter connecting gallery exists. Tautness between points is defined using their containing facets, and a gallery is minimal when it is taut between its extremities.

statements.title: Closed polysimplex and its facets
statements.statement_plain: A closed polysimplex is an affine set isomorphic to a finite product of closed simplices, with k at least 0 and every factor of positive dimension. statements.title: Convex Facet Maximality and Fixed-Point Chamber Correspondence
statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty convex subset X of the building, maximal facets meeting X all have the same dimension, and maximality is equivalent to maximizing the dimension of their intersections with X. In an apartment, a maximal facet meeting X spans every facet meeting X, and the affine span of its intersection with X contains the apartment's intersection with X. Applied to the convex Gamma-fixed building B, Gamma-chambers have equal dimension and correspond bijectively to chambers of B by intersection.
statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathcal{B}(G_K) be nonempty and convex, and let \mathfrak{F} consist either of all facets of \mathcal{B}(G_K) meeting X or of those facets in a fixed apartment A that meet X. Then all maximal facets in \mathfrak{F} have equal dimension, and F\in\mathfrak{F} is maximal exactly when \dim(F\cap X) is maximal. If F\subseteq A is maximal among the facets of A meeting X and A_F=\operatorname{Aff}(F), every facet of A meeting X lies in A_F and A\cap X\subseteq\operatorname{Aff}(F\cap X), so \dim(F\cap X)\geq\dim(F'\cap X) for every facet F' of A. For the nonempty convex subset \mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(G_K), all \Gamma\text{-chambers have equal dimension; for each \Gamma\text{-chamber }C, \mathcal{C}:=C^\Gamma=C\cap\mathcal{B} is a chamber of \mathcal{B}; conversely, each chamber \mathcal{C} of \mathcal{B} equals C\cap\mathcal{B} for the unique ambient facet C containing it, and that C is a \Gamma\text{-chamber}.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathcal{B}(G_K)\text{ is nonempty and convex.}
